name: Skool
tagline: Hosted communities, courses, events, gamification, and subscriptions

pricing.notes: Working normalization from the official public pricing structure. Recheck the source page immediately before publication.

tiers.name: Hobby
tiers.limits: Unlimited members, courses, videos and live calls; 10% transaction fee
tiers.notes: Yearly billing is advertised as 2 months free; annual-equivalent is $7.50/month ($90/year).

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.limits: Unlimited members, courses, videos and live calls; 2.9% transaction fee
tiers.notes: Yearly billing is advertised as 2 months free; annual-equivalent is $82.50/month ($990/year).

pricing.hiddenCosts: Skool takes a 10% transaction fee on Hobby or 2.9% on Pro from member payments; those fees are in addition to the subscription.

verdictSummary: Do not mistake the interface for the product. Skool's durable value is payments, network, compliance, which a solo one-shot build cannot reproduce responsibly. The prompt therefore builds only the closest honest personal consolation tool.
coreLoopDIY: Build a narrow community + courses storefront or member area for one creator, using Stripe Checkout and explicit digital-delivery rules.
diyTimeEstimate: not a true replacement; consolation build in one to two days
replacementScope: consolation build only; the paid product's moat remains
requirements: Stripe account and API keys in .env
Explicit README warning that this is a consolation build, not a production replacement
whatYouLose: tax, disputes, payouts, and fraud operations
whyPeopleStillPay: Skool: Creators pay to outsource payments, tax complexity, disputes, deliverability, moderation, and the trust needed to convert strangers.
ongoingBurden: Own payments, webhooks, refunds, tax records, fraud, access control, file delivery, moderation, backups, and support.

alternatives.name: Moodle
alternatives.desc: Courses, forums, events, badges and paid enrolment replace most of Skool; the cheerful leaderboard becomes academic furniture.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Discourse
rejectedAlternatives.desc: A first-rate forum with badges; courses and subscriptions remain conspicuously absent.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Odoo Community
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Courses, forums, events and checkout exist, but only after turning a business suite into a community site.

notes: Credibility row: Skool survives for a structural reason, not because its interface is difficult to copy.
prompt:
Build the closest honest consolation tool inspired by Skool; do not claim to replace its structural moat.
Use exactly this stack: Next.js 15 + TypeScript + PostgreSQL + Stripe.
Primary job: Build a narrow community + courses storefront or member area for one creator, using Stripe Checkout and explicit digital-delivery rules.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: marketplace discovery and buyer trust; tax, disputes, payouts, and fraud operations; native apps and community moderation.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
